meta.title: Who really said "We're on to Cincinnati"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Belichick really said it. The Patriots' own transcript records it three times at his 1 October 2014 presser, after a 41-14 loss to Kansas City.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We're on to Cincinnati'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Bill Belichick said it three times verbatim at Gillette Stadium on 1 October 2014. The date and the setting are what most retellings get wrong.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: Born 16 April 1952 · New England Patriots head coach, 2000–2023
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in a primary source: the New England Patriots’ own transcript of Belichick’s press conference at Gillette Stadium on Wednesday, 1 October 2014 records the sentence “We’re on to Cincinnati.” three times verbatim, plus two answers of “We’re getting ready for Cincinnati.” It was his stonewall response to questions about the Patriots’ 41–14 loss to Kansas City two nights earlier.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bill Belichick Press Conference Transcript: ‘We’re on to Cincinnati’
Press conference, Gillette Stadium, Foxborough — Wednesday, 1 October 2014
“We’re on to Cincinnati.” three times verbatim, plus “We’re getting ready for Cincinnati.” twice

source.excerpt:
Q: Your team has been successful for so long. How difficult is it to adjust to the adversity of Monday night’s game and get back on track?
BB: We’re on to Cincinnati.
Q: You mentioned Tom Brady’s age at the draft –
BB: We’re on to Cincinnati.
Q: Do you think having a 37-year old –
BB: We’re on to Cincinnati. It’s nothing about the past, nothing about the future. Right now we’re preparing for Cincinnati.
trail: Monday 29 September 2014 — the Kansas City Chiefs beat New England 41–14 on Monday Night Football, the loss that set the week’s agenda (2014 Patriots season ↗).

Wednesday 1 October 2014 — at his regular midweek press conference at Gillette Stadium, Belichick answers five consecutive questions about the loss by redirecting to the next opponent; the Patriots publish the transcript under the headline the phrase earned (Patriots.com ↗).
Sunday 5 October 2014 — New England beats the Bengals 43–17 at Gillette Stadium, and the line turns from stonewall into slogan (2014 Patriots season ↗).
September 2015 — Belichick explains himself on camera for NFL Films’ Do Your Job: “24 hours after the game, you’ve got to move on” (CBS Boston ↗).
source.excerptNote: Transcribed and published by the New England Patriots. The deflections continue past this point: asked whether he had done enough to help Tom Brady, Belichick answered “We’re getting ready for Cincinnati. That’s what we’re doing.”

author.name: Bill Belichick
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: Born 16 April 1952 · New England Patriots head coach 2000–2023 · six Super Bowl titles as head coach
author.bio: Bill Belichick coached the New England Patriots for 24 seasons, winning six Super Bowls — the record for a head coach — before the two sides parted ways in January 2024. He then became head coach of the North Carolina Tar Heels. His podium style is its own genre: flat, minimal, and famously allergic to any question about a game already played, which is exactly what produced this line.

misattribution.heading: What the retellings get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is solid — this is one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives contact with a primary source intact. What drifts is everything around the line: when it was said, where, and how many times.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ cites it as “Press Conference, September 29, 2014.” That is the date of the Kansas City game. The Patriots’ own transcript is captioned “his press conference at Gillette Stadium on Wednesday, October 1, 2014.”

The Enquirer’s retrospective calls it “the post-game press conference” (via Fox19 ↗). It was his routine midweek presser two days later — he opened it with a long, unprompted scouting report on the Bengals before any reporter spoke.

CBS Boston ↗ says he delivered it “13 times.” In the official transcript the sentence “We’re on to Cincinnati.” appears exactly three times, followed by two answers of “We’re getting ready for Cincinnati.” — five straight deflections in all, which is the count Wikiquote ↗ gives.
It is routinely shortened to “On to Cincinnati.” Belichick’s actual sentence begins with the pronoun: “We’re on to Cincinnati.”

misattribution.truthLine: He really said it, on the record, and his own team published the proof: the sentence is right there, three times, in the Patriots’ transcript of 1 October 2014 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: On Monday night, 29 September 2014, the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Patriots 41–14 on national television. Tom Brady was benched in the fourth quarter. The consensus that week was that New England’s dynasty had finally run out. When Belichick took the podium on the Wednesday, the reporters — led, per Wikipedia’s account of the week, by Albert Breer — wanted him to litigate all of it: the collapse, Brady’s age, whether the roster was good enough. He opened instead with an unbroken scouting report on the Bengals, and then simply refused.

The Patriots beat Cincinnati 43–17 the following Sunday and won the Super Bowl that season, which is why the line stopped being a deflection and became a slogan — printed on shirts, borrowed by politicians, and reused by Brady himself on social media after a later loss to Kansas City.
context.detailsSummary: What Belichick said about it afterwards
detailsBody: Interviewed for the NFL Films documentary Do Your Job: Bill Belichick and the 2014 New England Patriots, he was unapologetic: “I could have done it three times. I could have done it 53 times. It could have been 103 times if that’s what they wanted to keep asking because we had to turn the page,” he said in a preview quoted by the Cincinnati Enquirer ↗.
In another clip from the same documentary, reported by CBS Boston ↗ in September 2015, he added: “24 hours after the game, you’ve got to move on.”
context.pull: “It’s nothing about the past, nothing about the future. Right now we’re preparing for Cincinnati.”

sourcesVerified.claim: The Patriots' official transcript is captioned "his press conference at Gillette Stadium on Wednesday, October 1, 2014" and contains "We're on to Cincinnati." three times verbatim plus "We're getting ready for Cincinnati." twice, including the answer "We're on to Cincinnati. It's nothing about the past, nothing about the future. Right now we're preparing for Cincinnati."

Week 4 of 2014: Chiefs 41, Patriots 14 on 29 September; Week 5: Patriots 43, Bengals 17 on 5 October; and "In his regular press conference the ensuing Wednesday, when asked about the loss (primarily by Albert Breer), Belichick replied several times with his now famous line, 'We're on to Cincinnati'."

Wikiquote lists "We're on to Cincinnati." in its Quotes (sourced) section, dates it "Press Conference, September 29, 2014", and notes he repeated it five times in response to questions by Albert Breer about the 41-14 loss to Kansas City, with the Bengals as the next opponent (won 43-17).

CBS Boston (2 September 2015) states Belichick delivered "We're on to Cincinnati" "13 times", and quotes him from the NFL Films documentary Do Your Job: "24 hours after the game, you've got to move on."

Fox19/Cincinnati Enquirer (11 January 2024) calls it "the post-game press conference", says he asserted the phrase "five times", says he mentioned Cincinnati 15 times, states the Patriots went on to win the Super Bowl that season, and quotes Belichick: "I could have done it (repeated the phrase) three times. I could have done it 53 times. It could have been 103 times if that's what they wanted to keep asking because we had to turn the page."

Bill Belichick was born 16 April 1952, was head coach of the New England Patriots 2000-2023, holds the record of six Super Bowl wins as a head coach, and is now head coach of the North Carolina Tar Heels.
Bleacher Report's contemporaneous article (1 October 2014) describes it as "his Wednesday press conference", confirming the midweek rather than post-game setting.
